newsitem.title: QATAR: Gas bubble lifts Qatar into limelight.
newsitem.headline: Gas bubble lifts Qatar into limelight.

text.p: The gas plants and export berths at Qatar's new Ras Laffan industrial city represent the biggest potential shake-up to the Gulf Arab state's economy since it stumbled upon oil 60 years ago.

Running on supplies from the giant offshore North Field, liquefied natural gas plants at Ras Laffan, 56 miles north of the Qatari capital Doha, are Qatar's launch pad in its goal to become a leading gas exporter.

Qatargas -- a $6 billion venture between the Qatar General Petroleum Corp, Mobil Corp., France's Total SA and two Japanese firms, Mitsui and Marubeni -- exported its first LNG tanker from Ras Laffan to Japan in December.
By the end of 1998 Qatargas will be meeting contracts worth an annual 6 million metric tons of LNG to Japanese power firms.

A second plant, operated by the Rasgas joint venture of U.S., Japanese and South Korean firms, will begin LNG deliveries to South Korea in 1999 and a third plant being promoted by Enron Corp. is expected to start up around 2001.

"Qatar's strategy to shift from an oil to a gas economy, combined with a separate development of the huge North Field through different projects, offers great prospects for growth," said Marie-Francoise Chabrelie, general secretary of French CEDIGAZ, an international gas association body.
Qatar's population of 600,000 can expect an annual windfall of $1.6 billion in 2000 as Qatargas and Rasgas boost state revenue by nearly 65 percent, according to an International Monetary Fund study.
But though Ras Laffan is Qatar's best shot to escape persistent budget deficits and weak oil prices, it will not all be clear sailing for the new gas export industry.

Qatargas's sole Japanese customer, Chubu Electric Power Co., which took delivery of Qatar's first LNG export cargo in January, has already pressed for a review of prices agreed in 1992, while Rasgas has been forced to drop a minimum price provision with its client Korea Gas Corp.

Enron's plans for Qatar's third LNG plant, which envisaged exports to Israel and Jordan, have also been hampered by the deterioration in the Middle East peace process, although the Houston firm is now lining up sales contracts to India.
Hopes that the lucrative European gas market could be supplied will also be an uphill task given expected growth in Russian, North Sea and Algeria gas output.
The crux of Qatar's problem lies in LNG prices still being linked to volatile and weak oil prices and competing supplies from projects popping up from the Gulf, West Africa and Asia.

"This huge project (Qatargas) will not be the big money-spinner many believe it is if the price of oil drops," said former Saudi oil minister Sheikhh Ahmed Zaki Yamani. He forecast that oil prices were likely to be capped until the year 2001 because of growing world supply.
Qatargas's current bottom line, helped by the oil condensates produced through gas production at North Field, is an oil price of $11.50 a barrel, according to Yamani.
Oil prices are running around $20 a barrel.

Soft oil prices could also hurt Qatar's ability to meet heavy loan servicing from its share in the LNG projects and the needs of its equity partners and the U.S. investment and insurance companies that have ploughed $1.2 billion into the Middle East's largest bond offering.
Qatari officials concede that minimum LNG sales prices cannot be guaranteed.

But they pin their hopes on the huge resources of the North Field to catapult it into the gas major leagues by supporting a host of LNG, petrochemical, condensate refinery and synthetic fuel projects.

The North Field, one of the world's largest offshore fields not associated with an oilfield, covers more than 6,000 square kms (2,300 square miles) of Qatar's waters and its 373 trillion cubic feet (11 trillion cubic meters) of proven reserves, enough to last 400 years.
Qatar's Energy Minister Abdullah bin Hamad Al-Attiyah sees 12 million tons a year of LNG exports by the end of the decade, rising to an eventual capacity of 30 million tons.
"What is exciting about this country is that they are going in for large investment income...they are reaching a new stage of development," a Doha-based diplomat said.
